concepts.definition: Some French words are already familiar from cafés, films and travel.
Say {bonjour} when you arrive and {au revoir} when you leave. Add please when you ask for something, and thank you when you get it.
These words already make whole replies. Each one answers a question on its own.
A subject pronoun says who does the action: I, you, he, we or they.
Each pronoun for one person has a partner for more than one. {Ils} is for men or a mixed group, {elles} only for women.

examples.en: they, men or a mixed group

concepts.definition: Say {tu} to a friend, a child or family. Say {vous} to someone you do not know, or to more than one person.

examples.note: to a friend, a child or family
to someone you do not know, or to a group

concepts.definition: In conversation French speakers say {on} for we more often than {nous}. It takes the same verb form as {il} and {elle}.

examples.en: we, in conversation; also people in general
we, in writing and careful speech

concepts.definition: The verb for who you are and how you are. It is the verb French uses most.
Each person has its own form of {être}, so learn the pronoun and the verb together. {Elle est} and {elles sont} go like {il est} and {ils sont}.

concepts.term: {être} with a word or a name
concepts.definition: Use it with a describing word, as in I am happy, or with your name, as in I am Paul.
With the words from the first lesson, you can already answer a waiter.
The verb for what you have. French also uses it to give your age.
Before a vowel sound, {je} drops its e and joins the verb with an apostrophe. Before a consonant it stays as it is.
Use {avoir} for what someone has. French gives your age with it too: it says I have 20 years for I am 20.

concepts.term: A noun comes with an article
concepts.definition: In French a noun almost never stands alone. You say a coffee or the coffee, not just coffee.
Use {un} or {une} for any one thing, not a particular one. {Un} goes with a masculine noun and {une} with a feminine one.
Use {le} or {la} for one particular thing. {Les} is for more than one, and {l'} replaces both before a vowel.
Every noun is masculine or feminine, and its article must match. {Café} is masculine: it takes {un} and {le}.

concepts.term: Every noun is masculine or feminine
concepts.definition: Nothing in most nouns shows their gender, so learn each one with its article.
Put a noun after {avoir} to say what someone has, or after {c'est} to say what something is.

concepts.term: Every sentence uses a verb you know
concepts.definition: Each sentence in this lesson puts a new noun with {être} or {avoir}.
To say who someone is with a noun, put {un} or {une} before the noun. For he is or she is, French usually says {c'est}.

items/i-j-ai-un-livre.hint: Combine {avoir} + article + noun - all from earlier lessons!

mistakes.feedback: livre is masculine, use '{un}' not 'une'
Use '{un}' (a), not 'le' (the)

vocabulary/c-est-fr.note: point at something and name it: {c'est une maison}, {c'est un chat}

concepts.definition: Most nouns add -s in the plural, as in English. The s is silent, so you hear the plural in the article.
{Les} is the for more than one. {Des} is the plural of a: English often says nothing there, or some.
Every sentence in this lesson puts a plural noun after a verb you know.

items/i-elles-ont-les-chiens.situation: they have the dogs (all women or girls)
items/i-elles-ont-les-chiens.hint: Use {elles ont}, then {les} for the dogs.

mistakes.feedback: Use '{les}' (the), not 'des' (some)

concepts.definition: {Et} joins two words or two ideas.

examples.fr: J'ai un livre et un chat.
examples.en: I have a book and a cat.

concepts.definition: {Mais} sets one idea against another.

examples.fr: J'ai un chat, mais il a un chien.
examples.en: I have a cat, but he has a dog.

examples.fr: Je suis un homme, mais tu es une femme.
examples.en: I am a man, but you are a woman.

concepts.definition: {Ou} offers a choice between two things.

examples.fr: C'est un ami ou une amie ?
examples.en: Is it a male or a female friend?

concepts.definition: {Aussi} adds one more thing to what you said. It usually comes at the end.
{Très} makes a describing word stronger. It goes right before it.
These five words join the nouns and verbs you know into longer sentences.

examples.fr: Nous avons une maison et une voiture.
examples.en: We have a house and a car.

examples.fr: Le café est très bon, merci.
examples.en: The coffee is very good, thank you.

concepts.definition: {Ça} means that or it in everyday speech. You hear it in almost every conversation.
These four words mean this or that, and in the plural these or those. Each one goes before a noun.
The noun decides: its gender, its number and the sound it starts with.
Put the word before any noun you know to point at it.
{Ça} points at a thing without naming it. It is how people say that or it in conversation.
{C'est ça} says yes, that's right. People use it to agree or to confirm.
{Ça va ?} asks how someone is, and {ça va} answers it. It is the usual greeting between people who know each other.
{Ça} works with {être} and {avoir} the way a noun does.

items/i-c-est-ca.situation: Someone shows you what they meant. Confirm by saying 'that's it'

mistakes.feedback: Wrong order - use: c'est ça

concepts.definition: A word such as {ce} or {le} goes before the noun and matches its gender and number.
Every sentence in this lesson puts one of these noun groups after {être} or {avoir}.
The pronoun comes first, then the verb, then the noun with its word before it, as in English.
The verb for wanting a thing or wanting to do something. It is also how you ask for things politely.

examples.en: We want to have a house.

examples.fr: Ça va ? Tu veux un café ?
examples.en: How are you? Do you want a coffee?

concepts.definition: The stem changes three times: once for the singular, once for we and you, and once for they.
Put a second verb straight after {vouloir} to say what you want to do. The second verb does not change.

examples.en: I want to have a cat.
She wants to have a house.

conjugation.note: {vouloir} has three stems and four spoken forms. {veux}, {veut} and {veulent} change the stem; {voulons} and {voulez} keep the stem of {vouloir}.

items/i-elle-veut-etre-une-amie.gloss: She wants to be a friend

items/i-nous-voulons-avoir-une-maison.gloss: We want to have a house

concepts.definition: The verb for what someone can do: ability, chance and permission. It is one of the verbs French uses most.

examples.fr: Je peux avoir ça, s'il vous plaît ?
Je peux avoir ça, s'il te plaît ?

concepts.definition: The stem changes three times: once for the singular, once for we and you, and once for they.
Put a second verb straight after {pouvoir} to say what someone can do.

items/i-ils-peuvent-avoir-un.situation: Say that they are allowed to have a dog.
items/i-ils-peuvent-avoir-un.hint: Use {ils peuvent}, then {avoir} as it is.

mistakes.feedback: This needs {pouvoir}: {ils peuvent avoir un chien}.
{ils} takes {peuvent}: {ils peuvent avoir un chien}.

items/i-tu-peux-avoir-un.situation: Your friend asks if a cat is allowed. Say yes, she can have one.
items/i-tu-peux-avoir-un.hint: Use {tu peux}, then {avoir} as it is.

mistakes.feedback: This needs {pouvoir}: {tu peux avoir un chat}.
After {pouvoir} the second verb stays as it is: {tu peux avoir un chat}.

concepts.definition: The verb for seeing. It often comes after {vouloir}, as in {je veux voir}, I want to see.
The stem has a y for we and you, and an i everywhere else.
Put what you see after the verb, as in English.
{Voir} works with people too: put a name or a noun after it.

concepts.term: Three ways to ask a question
concepts.definition: French can ask the same question three ways. In speech the easiest are {est-ce que} and a rising voice.

examples.fr: Est-ce que tu as un chat ?

examples.note: with the verb first, more formal

concepts.definition: Put {est-ce que} before a statement to make it a question. The other words keep their order.

examples.fr: Est-ce que tu veux un café ?
Est-ce que vous voyez la maison ?

concepts.definition: Put the question word first, then {est-ce que}, then the statement.

examples.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu veux ça ?

concepts.definition: Say the statement and let your voice rise at the end. It is the most common way to ask in conversation.
Put the verb before the pronoun and join them with a hyphen. It sounds formal and is used most in writing.
These words ask who, where, when, how, why, and how much or how many.
{Que} starts a question. {Quoi} ends one or stands on its own.
Some questions are so common that people say them as one block.

items/i-est-ce-que-elle.situation: Ask "is she a woman?" using est-ce que method
items/i-est-ce-que-elle.hint: Put {est-ce qu'} before {elle est une femme}: {que} drops its e before a vowel.

mistakes.feedback: Add '{est-ce que}' at the beginning to make it a question!

checks.ask: Which one turns {Tu as un chat} into a question?

options.text: Est-ce que tu as un chat ?
Tu est-ce que as un chat ?
Tu as un chat est-ce que ?

checks.why: {Est-ce que} goes in front, and the rest of the sentence stays the same.

checks.ask: Listen. How is this question made?
checks.why: The words are the same as the statement. The voice rises at the end.

checks.ask: Which one is the formal question?
checks.why: The verb comes first, joined to {tu} with a hyphen: {Es-tu fatigué ?}

parts/p-est-ce-que.heading: {Est-ce que}
text: {Est-ce que} means roughly “is it that”. Put it in front of any statement and the statement becomes a question.

build.fr: Est-ce que tu as un chat ?

lines: Quand est-ce que tu veux un café ?
When do you want a coffee?
Combien de livres est-ce que tu as ?
How many books do you have?
blocks.heading: With a question word in front

parts/p-flip-the-verb.heading: Flip the verb
text: For formal speech and writing, put the verb before the subject and join them with a hyphen. This is called inversion.
parts/p-flip-the-verb.note: You will see it in books, formal emails and the news.

parts/p-raise-your-voice.heading: Raise your voice
text: In everyday speech, French speakers often keep the statement as it is and raise their voice at the end.
parts/p-raise-your-voice.note: Same words, different tone. This is how friends talk to each other.

concepts.definition: These pronouns stand on their own, come after a word such as {avec}, or add weight to who you mean.
Use them after a word such as {avec}, after {c'est}, and on their own as a one-word answer.
Subject pronouns go before the verb. Stressed pronouns go after a preposition.
{bien que} says you do something despite another fact. The verb after it takes the special form.

examples.fr: Bien que je sois fatigué, je travaille.
Bien qu'elle soit malade, elle vient.

concepts.definition: The second half of the sentence says what happens anyway.

examples.fr: Bien qu'il fasse froid, on va au parc.
examples.en: Even though it's cold, we're going to the park.

examples.fr: Bien que je sois fatigué, je t'aide pour que tu partes avant qu'il soit trop tard.
examples.en: Although I'm tired, I'm helping you so you can leave before it's too late.

concepts.definition: Small words such as with, in or under that link a noun or a pronoun to the rest of the sentence.
These say where something is: on, under, in front of, behind or between.

examples.fr: Le livre est derrière la porte.
examples.en: The book is behind the door.

concepts.definition: These link people and places: with, for, at, to and from.
After a preposition, use a stressed pronoun such as {moi}, never a subject pronoun such as {je}.
Put the preposition and its noun after the verb, as in English.

examples.fr: Le chat est sous la table.
examples.en: The cat is under the table.
I am in front of the house.

concepts.definition: An adjective takes the gender of the noun it describes. Most add an -e for a feminine noun.
Most adjectives add -e for the feminine, as {petit} does. A few change more, as {nouveau} and {vieux} do.
A few adjectives, such as {jeune} and {autre}, have one form for both genders.
These common adjectives go before the noun, while most French adjectives go after it.
Before a masculine noun that starts with a vowel sound, three of these adjectives change form so the words run together. Feminine forms stay the same.
{avant que} sets your action before someone else's. The verb after it takes the special form.
Use it to say what has to happen first.

examples.fr: Avant que tu partes, parlons en mangeant.
examples.en: Before you leave, let's talk while we eat.

concepts.definition: These words say how you do something. Many end in -ment, as many English ones end in -ly.
Some of these words go before a describing word to make it stronger.

2024-01-22-reading2.description: An exciting trip through beautiful Normandy! Explore famous places with the words you know so far.

passage/b-ca-c-est-un.speaker: Marie
passage/b-ca-c-est-un.fr: Ça ? C'est un livre sur la Normandie. Mont-Saint-Michel, Rouen... Ces choses sont très belles !
passage/b-ca-c-est-un.en: That? It's a book about Normandy. Mont-Saint-Michel, Rouen... These things are very beautiful!

2024-01-22-reading2.title: Reading Comprehension - {Rendez-vous en Normandie}

concepts.term: A different form after {il faut que}
concepts.definition: After phrases like {il faut que}, the verb takes a special form, called the subjunctive. It shows a need, a wish or a feeling about what someone does.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu sois gentil.

concepts.definition: They come after a phrase that ends in {que} and names a need, a wish or a feeling.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu fasses ça.
Il faut qu'il aille à Paris.
examples.en: He needs to go to Paris.

concepts.definition: In an ordinary statement or question, use the ordinary form.
When {que} and a person follow {il faut}, the verb after them takes the special form.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu sois là.
Il faut qu'il ait le livre.
examples.en: He needs to have the book.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu ailles au café.
examples.en: You need to go to the café.

vocabulary/il-faut-que-fr.gloss: it's necessary that / someone needs to
vocabulary/il-faut-que-fr.note: from {falloir}; the verb after it takes the forms in this lesson

concepts.definition: These verbs change the same way after {il faut que} and phrases like it.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu saches ça.

concepts.definition: Use the special form after {que} in a phrase of need, wish or feeling. Everywhere else, use the ordinary form.
With {que} and a person after {il faut}, the verb changes. Without them, it does not.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu partes maintenant.

2024-01-24-unit2-exam.description: Test everything from this unit! Demonstratives, essential verbs (vouloir/pouvoir/voir), questions, stressed pronouns, prepositions, and descriptive sentences.

items/i-elles-sont-chez-laduree.hint: elles sont + chez + Ladurée (famous macaron shop)

concepts.definition: {De} with {le} becomes {du}. With {les} it becomes {des}, but {de la} stays as it is.
{À} with {le} becomes {au}. With {les} it becomes {aux}, but {à la} stays as it is.

examples.fr: Je suis au café avec eux.
examples.en: I'm at the café with them.

examples.fr: Le chat est à la maison.

concepts.definition: The same words also mean some, for an amount you do not count. English often leaves the word out.
Before a vowel sound, {de} and {à} take {l'} for both genders.
After a feeling and {que}, the verb takes the special form.

examples.fr: Je suis content que tu sois là.
Je suis triste que tu partes.
Je regrette que tu ne puisses pas venir.
Il faut que tu viennes : je veux que tu sois là !
examples.en: You have to come: I want you to be there!

concepts.definition: Happy, sad, afraid, sorry and surprised all work the same way.

examples.fr: Je suis désolé que tu sois malade.
Je suis surpris que tu saches ça.
J'ai peur qu'elle ne comprenne pas.

concepts.term: Same person: {de} and a verb, not {que}
concepts.definition: When the feeling and the action belong to the same person, use {de} and the verb as it is. Use {que} and the special form for someone else's action.

examples.fr: Je suis content de te voir.
Je suis content que tu sois là.

examples.note: {de} also follows {c'est} and a describing word

vocabulary/je-suis-content-que-tu-sois-l.fr: je suis content que tu sois là

concepts.definition: {j'avais déjà} with a past verb shows that one thing happened before another thing in the past.

examples.fr: Quand il est arrivé, j'avais déjà mangé.
examples.en: When he arrived, I had already eaten.
I had already seen this movie.

concepts.definition: {déjà} usually goes between the two parts of the verb.
The verb for coming and arriving. You hear it all the time in conversation.
The stem changes three times: once for the singular, once for we and you, and once for they, which doubles the n.
Like other verbs, {venir} can come straight after {vouloir} or {pouvoir}.

examples.en: I can come to the hotel.

concepts.definition: Adding re- to a verb often means again or back, so {revenir} means to come back. Its forms are the forms of {venir} with re- in front.

vocabulary/tu-viens-me-voir-fr.gloss: are you coming to see me?

concepts.definition: The verb for going somewhere. With a second verb after it, it also says what is going to happen.
Almost every form is different, so learn each one with its pronoun.
Put a second verb after {aller} to say what is going to happen, as in English.

examples.en: What are you going to have?

items/i-qu-est-ce-que-2.situation: Ask what someone is going to have
items/i-qu-est-ce-que-2.cue: What are you going to have?

mistakes.feedback: This needs aller! Try: qu'est-ce que tu vas avoir?

concepts.definition: {si} with a past form, like {j'étais}, talks about something that is not real.

examples.fr: Si on avait le temps, on marcherait.
examples.en: If we had time, we'd walk.

concepts.definition: If I were you: a common way to give advice.

examples.fr: Si j'étais toi, je ferais ça.
examples.en: If I were you, I'd do that.

2024-01-27-hypothetical-phrases.description: Talk about fantasies and what-ifs! '{Si j'étais riche...}' (If I were rich...), '{Si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais}' (If I had time, I'd travel). Everyone loves daydreaming!

concepts.definition: {il faut} with a verb says what has to be done in general. {il faut que} with a person says who has to do it.

examples.fr: Il faut qu'on aille au parc.
examples.en: We need to go to the park.

concepts.definition: Parents and friends say these phrases every day.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu sois sage.
Il faut que tu fasses attention.

vocabulary/il-faut-que-tu-fasses-attenti.fr: il faut que tu fasses attention

vocabulary/il-faut-que-tu-sois-sage-fr.fr: il faut que tu sois sage

checks.ask: Listen. Do {je veux} and {il veut} sound the same?
checks.why: They sound the same. The x and the t at the end are both silent.

checks.ask: Listen. In {ils veulent}, do you hear the -ent?
checks.why: The -ent is written but not spoken.

checks.ask: Which verb breaks the -ons ending for {nous}?
checks.why: {nous sommes}. {avoir} and {aller} keep it: {nous avons}, {nous allons}.

parts/p-the-silent-ent.heading: The silent -ent
text: For {ils} and {elles}, the verb ends in -ent.
parts/p-the-silent-ent.note: The -ent is written but not spoken. In writing, it tells you that several people are doing something. It can change how the letters before it sound, so {ils veulent} sounds a little different from {il veut}.

list: Different spellings often share one sound, so the forms you hear keep coming back.
{être}, {avoir} and {aller} are among the most irregular verbs in French, and you know them already.
Most verbs you meet next follow these patterns, starting with the verb for 'to leave' in the next lesson.

concepts.definition: {je pense que} says what you believe is true. The verb after it keeps its ordinary form.

examples.fr: Je pense que c'est bon de partir tôt.
examples.en: I think it's good to leave early.

concepts.definition: When you doubt something, the verb after {que} takes the special form.

examples.fr: Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne.
Je ne crois pas qu'il ait raison.

concepts.definition: {Je ne pense pas que} sounds gentler than a plain no.

examples.fr: Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai.
Je doute que ce soit possible.

items/i-c-est-bon-de-partir.text: Marie veut partir tôt. Je pense que c'est bon ___ partir tôt.
items/i-c-est-bon-de-partir.gloss: Marie wants to leave early. I think it's good to leave early.

concepts.definition: The verb for leaving a place or setting off on a trip.

concepts.term: The t you hear only in the plural
concepts.definition: In the singular forms you hear no t. In the plural forms the t comes back and is heard.
{Partir} goes straight after the verbs for wanting, being able and going.

conjugation.note: {partir} drops its t in {je pars}, {tu pars} and {il part}, where you hear no t. The t comes back, and is heard, in {ils partent}, {vous partez} and {nous partons}.

items/i-elle-part-avec-qui.hint: The form of {partir} for {elle}, then {avec qui}.
items/i-elle-part-avec-qui.situation: Your sister is leaving the party. Ask who she is leaving with.

mistakes.feedback: With {elle} it is {part}, like {il part}.

items/i-il-part-avec-elle.hint: The form of {partir} for {il}, then {avec elle}.
items/i-il-part-avec-elle.situation: Someone asks where your brother is. He is leaving with your sister.

mistakes.feedback: With {il} it is {part}, ending in a t you do not hear.

items/i-je-pars-avec-toi.hint: The form of {partir} for {je}, then {avec toi}.
items/i-je-pars-avec-toi.situation: Your friend asks if you are coming to the café. You are leaving, and you want her to come too.

mistakes.feedback: With {je} it is {pars}, with an s you do not hear.

items/i-je-peux-partir-avec-vous.hint: {je peux}, then the whole verb and {avec vous}.
items/i-je-peux-partir-avec-vous.situation: Your teacher is leaving too. Tell her you can leave with her, politely.

mistakes.feedback: After {peux}, the verb stays whole: {partir}.

items/i-je-vais-partir-en-normandie.situation: A friend asks about your summer.
items/i-je-vais-partir-en-normandie.cue: I'm going to leave for Normandy

mistakes.feedback: After {vais}, the verb stays whole: {partir}.

items/i-je-veux-partir.situation: It is late and you are tired. Tell your friends.

mistakes.feedback: After {veux}, the verb stays whole: {partir}.

items/i-nous-partons-en-normandie.hint: The form of {partir} for {nous}, then {en Normandie}.
items/i-nous-partons-en-normandie.situation: A neighbour asks about your weekend plans. Your family is going to Normandy.

mistakes.feedback: With {nous} it is {partons}: the t comes back.

items/i-pourquoi-ils-partent.hint: {pourquoi est-ce que}, then the form of {partir} for {ils}.
items/i-pourquoi-ils-partent.situation: Your neighbours are packing their car. Ask why they are leaving.

mistakes.feedback: With {ils} it is {partent}: the t comes back, and you hear it.

items/i-pourquoi-tu-veux-partir.hint: {pourquoi est-ce que}, then {tu veux} and the whole verb.
items/i-pourquoi-tu-veux-partir.situation: Your friend says she does not like the party. Ask her why she wants to leave.
items/i-pourquoi-tu-veux-partir.cue: Why do you want to leave?
items/i-pourquoi-tu-veux-partir.answer: pourquoi est-ce que tu veux partir ?

mistakes.answer: pourquoi est-ce que tu veux pars ?
mistakes.feedback: After {veux}, the verb stays whole: {partir}.

items/i-quand-tu-pars.hint: {quand est-ce que}, then the form of {partir} for {tu}.
items/i-quand-tu-pars.situation: Your friend has her coat on. Ask her when she is leaving.

mistakes.feedback: With {tu} it is {pars}, like {je pars}.

items/i-quand-tu-vas-partir.hint: {quand est-ce que}, then {tu vas} and the whole verb.
items/i-quand-tu-vas-partir.situation: Your friend says she is going away. Ask her when.
items/i-quand-tu-vas-partir.cue: When are you going to leave?
items/i-quand-tu-vas-partir.answer: quand est-ce que tu vas partir ?

mistakes.answer: quand est-ce que tu vas pars ?
mistakes.feedback: After {vas}, the verb stays whole: {partir}.

items/i-tu-peux-partir.situation: Your friend has a train to catch. Ask if she can leave now.

mistakes.feedback: After {peux}, the verb stays whole: {partir}.

concepts.definition: An object pronoun stands for the person or thing the action happens to: me, you, him, her, it, us or them.
French puts the object pronoun before the verb, the other way round from English.
The subject does the action and the object receives it. {Il} is he, and {le} is him.
{si j'avais} with a past verb talks about something you wish had gone differently.
The second half of the sentence says what would have happened.

examples.fr: Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
examples.en: If I'd known, I would have come.
If I'd studied, I would have succeeded.

items/i-elle-a-commence-a-parler.text: Au téléphone, ma mère a commencé ___ parler de son voyage.
items/i-elle-a-commence-a-parler.gloss: On the phone, my mother started to talk about her trip.

items/i-j-ai-decide-de-rester.text: J'étais malade, alors hier j'ai décidé ___ rester à la maison.

concepts.definition: These words say whose something is. They go right before the noun, where {le} or {un} would go.

examples.fr: Je vais au café avec mon ami.
examples.en: I'm going to the café with my friend.

concepts.definition: The possessive takes the gender and number of the thing owned, never of the owner.
Use the {tu} words for your with a friend, and the {vous} words with someone you do not know or with a group.
Our, your and their have no masculine or feminine forms. They change only for the plural.
My, your and his or her have three forms: masculine, feminine and plural. Our, your and their have two: singular and plural.

concepts.term: {il est possible que}: it might happen
concepts.definition: It says something might happen. The verb after it takes the special form.
A quick way to say you are not sure. With {que} after it, the verb keeps its ordinary form.
These phrases leave room to change a plan.

examples.fr: Il est possible qu'on parte demain.

concepts.definition: These stand on their own and mean mine, yours, his and so on. They take the place of a noun you already named.
A possessive pronoun always comes with its article, {le} or {la}.
Like the possessive adjectives, it agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.

2024-02-01-reading-10.description: A story about dreams and ambitions using this unit's advanced expressions: wishes (je veux que...), emotions (je suis content que...), hypotheticals (si j'étais...), and more

items/reading-10-8.cue: What did they decide to do?

passage/b-ah-oui-moi-aussi.fr: Il a dit: "Ah oui? Moi aussi, j'ai beaucoup de rêves. Je veux que ma vie change."
passage/b-ah-oui-moi-aussi.en: He said: "Oh yes? Me too, I have many dreams. I want my life to change."

passage/b-bonjour-marc-je-suis.fr: J'ai dit: "Bonjour Marc! Je suis heureuse que tu sois là. J'étais en train de penser à mes rêves."
passage/b-bonjour-marc-je-suis.en: I said: "Hello Marc! I'm happy you're here. I was thinking about my dreams."

passage/b-comme-marc-a-dit.fr: Comme Marc l'a dit: il faut essayer! Si on ne fait rien, on ne saura jamais. Et moi, je veux savoir si mes rêves peuvent devenir réalité.
passage/b-comme-marc-a-dit.en: Like Marc said: you have to try! If we don't do anything, we'll never know. And me, I want to know if my dreams can become reality.

passage/b-en-rentrant-chez-moi.fr: En rentrant chez moi, j'ai pensé à notre conversation. Avant, j'avais perdu espoir, et je le regrette. Mais maintenant, je suis contente que Marc soit mon ami.
passage/b-en-rentrant-chez-moi.en: Walking home, I thought about our conversation. Before, I had lost hope, and I regret it. But now, I'm glad Marc is my friend.

passage/b-il-faut-que-tu.fr: Il a dit: "Il faut que tu essaies encore! Si j'étais toi, je ne renoncerais pas."
passage/b-il-faut-que-tu.en: He said: "You have to try again! If I were you, I wouldn't give up."

passage/b-je-comprends-mais-il.fr: J'ai dit: "Je comprends. Mais il faut que tu essaies! Si tu ne fais rien, tu ne sauras jamais."
passage/b-je-comprends-mais-il.en: I said: "I understand. But you have to try! If you don't do anything, you'll never know."

passage/b-je-suis-content-que.fr: Marc a dit: "Je suis content que tu aies ce rêve. Tu serais une excellente professeur."
passage/b-je-suis-content-que.en: Marc said: "I'm glad you have this dream. You'd be an excellent teacher."

passage/b-je-suis-heureux-que.fr: Marc a dit: "Je suis heureux que nous soyons amis. On peut s'aider."
passage/b-je-suis-heureux-que.en: Marc said: "I'm happy we're friends. We can help each other."

passage/b-je-veux-qu-un.fr: Il a dit: "Je veux qu'un jour mes peintures soient au Louvre. Mais j'ai peur que ce soit difficile."
passage/b-je-veux-qu-un.en: He said: "I want my paintings to be at the Louvre one day. But I'm afraid it might be difficult."

passage/b-marc-m-a-dit.fr: Marc m'a parlé de son rêve: être artiste. Il voulait que les gens voient ses peintures au Louvre un jour. C'est un grand rêve! Le Louvre est le musée le plus célèbre du monde.
passage/b-marc-m-a-dit.en: Marc talked to me about his dream: to be an artist. He wanted people to see his paintings at the Louvre one day. It's a big dream! The Louvre is the most famous museum in the world.

passage/b-merci-mais-j-ai.fr: J'ai dit: "Merci! Mais j'ai peur que ce soit trop difficile. J'avais déjà essayé l'année dernière mais je n'ai pas réussi."
passage/b-merci-mais-j-ai.en: I said: "Thank you! But I'm afraid it might be too difficult. I had already tried last year but I didn't succeed."

passage/b-merci-marc-je-suis.fr: J'ai dit: "Merci Marc. Je suis reconnaissante que tu sois là pour moi. Toi aussi, tu dois continuer avec tes peintures."
passage/b-merci-marc-je-suis.en: I said: "Thank you Marc. I'm grateful you're here for me. You too, you must continue with your paintings."

passage/b-moi-aussi-j-aimerais.fr: J'ai dit: "Moi aussi! J'aimerais que nous réussissions tous les deux."
passage/b-moi-aussi-j-aimerais.en: I said: "Me too! I'd like us both to succeed."

passage/b-mon-ami-marc-est.fr: Mon ami Marc est arrivé au café. Il savait que j'aime ce café parce que c'est près de Notre-Dame. Je suis contente qu'il soit là! On se parle toujours de nos rêves.
passage/b-mon-ami-marc-est.en: My friend Marc arrived at the café. He knew I like this café because it's near Notre-Dame. I'm glad he's here! We always talk to each other about our dreams.

passage/b-nous-avons-decide-d.fr: Nous avons décidé de nous aider l'un l'autre. Je veux qu'il réussisse avec ses peintures, et il veut que je réussisse comme professeur.
passage/b-nous-avons-decide-d.en: We decided to help each other. I want him to succeed with his paintings, and he wants me to succeed as a teacher.

passage/b-nous-avons-parle-pendant.fr: Nous avons parlé pendant une heure. Je lui ai parlé de mon rêve: être professeur de français. J'aimerais que mes étudiants adorent la langue française comme moi.
passage/b-nous-avons-parle-pendant.en: We talked for an hour. I talked to him about my dream: to be a French teacher. I'd like my students to love the French language like me.

passage/b-oui-j-adore-paris.fr: J'ai dit: "Oui ! J'adore Paris la nuit. C'est pour ça que je veux rester ici toute ma vie."
passage/b-oui-j-adore-paris.en: I said: "Yes! I love Paris at night. That's why I want to stay here all my life."

passage/b-salut-sophie-je-savais.fr: Il a dit: "Salut Sophie! Je savais que tu serais ici."
passage/b-salut-sophie-je-savais.en: He said: "Hi Sophie! I knew you'd be here."

passage/b-si-on-avait-plus.fr: Marc a dit: "Si on avait plus de temps, on pourrait marcher toute la nuit."
passage/b-si-on-avait-plus.en: Marc said: "If we had more time, we could walk all night."

passage/b-sophie-il-faut-que.fr: Il a dit: "Sophie, il faut que tu saches une chose: tes rêves sont importants. Je veux que tu continues à essayer."
passage/b-sophie-il-faut-que.en: He said: "Sophie, you need to know one thing: your dreams are important. I want you to keep trying."

concepts.definition: The four points of the compass.
Phrases for left, right and straight ahead.
These phrases place one thing beside, across from, near or far from another.

examples.fr: C'est à côté de la gare.

examples.en: Go straight as far as the station, then turn left.

examples.fr: Elle donne de l'argent aux enfants.

examples.fr: Tu peux me donner ton numéro ?
examples.en: Can you give me your number?

concepts.definition: {donner} follows the -er pattern, like {parler}.
The thing comes straight after {donner}, and the person after {à}. As a pronoun, the person becomes {lui} and goes before the verb.

examples.fr: Je donne le livre à Marie.
examples.en: I give the book to Marie.

concepts.definition: When the thing you give becomes a pronoun like {le}, it goes after the person. Both pronouns stay before the verb.

examples.en: Will you give it to me?

examples.fr: Je te donne rendez-vous au café.

concepts.definition: English listens to something. In French, nothing goes between {écouter} and the thing.

You know {Regarde !} and {Écoute !} as commands. The same verbs work with every person.
{voir} is what your eyes take in. {regarder} is looking on purpose, and {écouter} is listening on purpose.

passage/b-paris-sa-capitale-compte.fr: Paris, sa capitale, a plus de deux millions d'habitants. Cette ville magnifique attire des millions de visiteurs chaque année. Ils viennent admirer ses monuments célèbres comme la Tour Eiffel, Notre-Dame, le Louvre, et l'Arc de Triomphe sur les Champs-Élysées. Beaucoup visitent aussi le château de Versailles. Les touristes cherchent souvent des directions pour trouver ces lieux historiques.
passage/b-paris-sa-capitale-compte.en: Paris, its capital, has more than two million inhabitants. This magnificent city attracts millions of visitors each year. They come to admire its famous monuments like the Eiffel Tower, Notre-Dame, the Louvre, and the Arc de Triomphe on the Champs-Élysées. Many also visit the Palace of Versailles. Tourists often look for directions to find these historic places.

concepts.definition: Use {que} when someone else does the action. The person or thing doing it comes after {que}.

examples.en: After work, I have a coffee.

concepts.definition: Short phrases that say when something happens or how often.

examples.fr: En ce moment, je suis à Paris.

concepts.definition: These words put actions in order. They usually start the sentence.
Without these words, short sentences sound choppy. With them, they sound like a story.

examples.fr: D'abord, je mange. Ensuite, je pars.
examples.en: First I eat. Then I leave.

concepts.definition: Words for order usually start the sentence. Words like {avant} and {après} go before a noun.

examples.fr: Je suis ici depuis ce matin.
examples.en: I've been here since this morning.

2024-05-25-unit-8-practice.title: Daily Life & Actions Practice - Fill in the Blanks

concepts.definition: The everyday word for because. It answers a question with {pourquoi}.

examples.fr: Pourquoi tu ne viens pas ? Parce que je suis fatigué.
examples.en: Why aren't you coming? Because I'm tired.

examples.fr: Je ne viens pas parce que je suis malade.
examples.en: I'm not coming because I'm sick.

examples.fr: Je mange parce que j'ai faim.

concepts.definition: {car} also means because, but it sounds more formal and is common in writing. It never starts a sentence.

examples.fr: On étudie le français car c'est beau.
examples.en: We study French because it's beautiful.

examples.fr: Je prends un café car je suis fatigué.
examples.en: I'm having a coffee because I'm tired.

concepts.definition: Use {puisque} when the reason is something you both already know.

examples.fr: Puisque tu es là, on commence.
Puisque c'est vrai, je te crois.
examples.en: Since it's true, I believe you.

concepts.definition: {comme} gives the reason at the start of a sentence.

examples.fr: Comme il fait beau, on va au parc.
examples.en: As it's nice out, we're going to the park.

examples.fr: Comme je suis fatigué, je vais dormir.
examples.en: As I'm tired, I'm going to sleep.

examples.fr: Comme c'est ton anniversaire, on va au restaurant.
examples.en: As it's your birthday, we're going to a restaurant.

concepts.definition: Use {grâce à} before a noun or a pronoun, for a reason that helped.

examples.fr: Grâce à toi, je comprends mieux.
examples.en: Thanks to you, I understand better.
I understand thanks to the teacher.

concepts.definition: Use {à cause de} before a noun, usually for a reason that caused a problem.

examples.fr: À cause de la musique, je ne peux pas travailler.
examples.en: Because of the music, I can't work.

examples.fr: Je suis en retard à cause du bus.
examples.en: I'm late because of the bus.

examples.fr: Je suis fatigué à cause du travail.

items/i-a-cause.text: ___ du travail, je ne peux pas venir
items/i-a-cause.gloss: Because of work, I can't come

mistakes.feedback: Work isn't a positive reason here. Use '{à cause de}'.
Parce que needs a CLAUSE: '{parce que j'ai du travail}'. Use '{à cause de}' + noun!

items/i-a-cause-de.text: ___ la musique, je ne peux pas travailler
items/i-a-cause-de.gloss: Because of the music, I can't work

mistakes.feedback: Parce que needs a CLAUSE: '{parce qu'il pleut}'. Use '{à cause de}' + noun here!
Grâce à is for POSITIVE reasons! Use '{à cause de}' for negative/neutral.

items/i-a-cause-du.gloss: I'm late because of the bus

mistakes.feedback: Parce que needs a CLAUSE: '{parce que le bus est en retard}'. Use '{à cause de}' + noun!
Being late isn't positive! Use '{à cause de}' for negative reasons.
Close! But '{à cause de}' + noun is more direct than parce que + clause.
Not sleeping well isn't positive! Use '{à cause de}' for problems.

items/i-car.text: On étudie le français ___ c'est beau
items/i-car.gloss: We study French for it's beautiful

mistakes.feedback: Parce que works! But '{car}' is more elegant in this context.
Comme must come at the START of the sentence: '{Comme c'est utile, on étudie...}'

items/i-grace-au.gloss: I understand thanks to the teacher

mistakes.feedback: Close! But '{grâce à}' + noun is more elegant than 'parce que' + clause here.
Succeeding is positive! Use '{grâce à}' for positive attribution.

items/i-parce-que-2.text: Pourquoi tu ne viens pas ? - ___ je suis fatigué
items/i-parce-que-2.gloss: Why aren't you coming? - Because I'm tired

mistakes.feedback: Car works but sounds formal. Use '{parce que}' to answer '{pourquoi}'.
Puisque is for known facts, not direct answers to '{pourquoi}'. Use '{parce que}'!

items/i-puisque-2.text: On va partir ___ tu es là

mistakes.feedback: Parce que works! But '{puisque}' emphasizes the logical conclusion better.
Car works but '{puisque}' is more natural for 'since'.

concepts.definition: Take the {nous} form of the present, drop -ons and add the imparfait endings. Every verb works this way except {être}.

examples.fr: Je parlais français tous les jours.
examples.en: I used to speak French every day.

concepts.definition: Start from the present {nous} form of the verb.
Take off the -ons, and what is left is the stem. The stem of {nous faisons} is fais-.

examples.fr: Je prenais le bus tous les jours.
examples.en: I used to take the bus every day.

examples.fr: On allait au café chaque samedi.
examples.en: We used to go to the café every Saturday.

concepts.definition: The endings are the same for every verb. Four of the six forms sound the same.
{être} uses the stem ét- instead. The endings are the same.
Use it to describe how things were and what you used to do.

examples.fr: Quand j'étais jeune, je jouais avec mon chien.
examples.en: When I was young, I used to play with my dog.

examples.fr: Il y avait beaucoup de gens.
examples.en: There were a lot of people.
She used to work a lot.

items/i-etais-2.text: Quand j'___ jeune, je jouais avec mon chien
items/i-etais-2.gloss: When I was young, I used to play with my dog

mistakes.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for description: j'étais jeune.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: j'étais (I was).
That's il/elle form! Use '{je}' form: j'étais (not était).

vocabulary/je-jouais-fr.gloss: I was playing / I used to play

concepts.definition: Says that something is close. Before a vowel, {de} becomes {d'}.

examples.fr: Le café est près de l'école.
examples.en: The café is near the school.

concepts.definition: Says that something is a long way away.

examples.fr: La gare est loin de la maison.
examples.en: The station is far from the house.

examples.fr: Le parc est loin de la ville.
examples.en: The park is far from the city.

concepts.definition: Says that something is right beside something else.

examples.fr: Je suis à côté de toi.
Le restaurant est à côté du cinéma.
examples.en: The restaurant is next to the cinema.

concepts.definition: Says that something faces something else.

examples.fr: Ma maison est en face du parc.
examples.en: My house is across from the park.

examples.fr: Il est assis en face de moi.

concepts.definition: Says that something is all around something else.

examples.fr: Les gens sont autour de la table.
Il y a un jardin autour de la maison.
examples.en: There's a garden around the house.

concepts.definition: Says that something follows the length of a street, a road or a river.

examples.fr: On marche le long de la rivière.
Il y a des arbres le long de la route.
examples.en: There are trees along the road.

concepts.term: {au milieu de} = in the middle of
concepts.definition: Says that something is in the center of a place.

examples.fr: Il y a une fontaine au milieu de la place.
examples.en: There's a fountain in the middle of the square.

examples.fr: La table est au milieu de la cuisine.
examples.en: The table is in the middle of the kitchen.

concepts.term: {au bout de} = at the end of
concepts.definition: Says that something is at the far end of a place.

examples.fr: Le restaurant est au bout de la rue.
examples.en: The restaurant is at the end of the street.

examples.fr: La porte est au bout du jardin.
examples.en: The door is at the end of the garden.

mistakes.feedback: Avec means 'with'. Use '{à côté de}' for physical position 'next to'!
Près de means 'near' (general). Use '{à côté de}' for 'right next to'!

items/i-au-bout-du.gloss: The door is at the end of the garden

mistakes.feedback: Dans means 'in' (general). Use '{au bout de}' for 'at the end of'!
Près de means 'near'. Use '{au bout de}' for 'at the end of'!

items/i-au-milieu-de-la.gloss: The table is in the middle of the kitchen

mistakes.feedback: Dans means 'in' (general). Use '{au milieu de}' for 'in the middle of'!
Sur means 'on'. Use '{au milieu de}' for 'in the middle of'!

concepts.definition: With {être}, the participle matches the subject: -e for feminine, -s for plural.
For a man, with {il}, the participle has no ending.

examples.fr: Mon frère est allé en France.

concepts.definition: For a woman, with {elle}, add -e. You do not hear it.

examples.fr: Ma mère est allée au marché.
examples.en: My mother went to the market.

examples.fr: Elle est montée dans le bus.

concepts.definition: For a group, add -s, as with {ils} or {nous}. You do not hear it either.

examples.fr: Paul et Marc sont rentrés tard.
examples.en: Paul and Marc came home late.

concepts.definition: For a group of women, add -es.

examples.fr: Mes sœurs sont allées à Paris.
Les filles sont arrivées hier soir.
Nous sommes restées à la maison.
Vous êtes allées où, les filles ?

concepts.definition: When a group has men and women, use the masculine -s.

examples.fr: Pierre et Marie sont partis ensemble.
Pierre et Marie sont allés au café.
examples.en: Pierre and Marie went to the café.

concepts.definition: With {avoir}, the participle does not change for the subject.

items/i-sont-rentres.gloss: Paul and Marc came home late

mistakes.feedback: Paul et Marc is plural! Add -s for masculine plural: {sont rentrés}.
Paul and Marc are men, so use -s (not -es): {sont rentrés}.
Rentrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's '{sont rentrés}', not 'ont rentrés'.

vocabulary/vous-etes-alle-fr.note: formal singular masculine; masculine singular (no change)

vocabulary/vous-etes-alles-fr.example_fr: Les enfants, vous êtes allés où ?

concepts.definition: The passé composé tells what happened. It is the present of {avoir} followed by a past participle.
Take off the -er and add -é. It sounds the same as the infinitive.
Only {avoir} changes with the person. The participle stays the same.
{ne} and {pas} go around the form of {avoir}, and the participle comes after them.

examples.fr: Je n'ai pas aimé le film.

concepts.definition: Ask with {est-ce que}, or put the form of {avoir} before the subject.

examples.en: Did you look for my book?
examples.note: the voice goes up at the end

concepts.definition: Use the passé composé for something that happened and is over, often at a time you name.

examples.fr: On a regardé un film hier soir.
examples.en: We watched a film last night.

items/i-a-regarde.gloss: We watched a film last night

mistakes.feedback: That's present tense! Use passé composé: on a regardé (we watched).
Change -er to -é! The past participle is '{regardé}', not 'regarder'.

items/i-avez-cherche.gloss: Did you look for my book?

mistakes.feedback: That's present tense! Use passé composé: vous avez cherché (you looked for).
Change -er to -é! The past participle is '{cherché}', not 'chercher'.
'Avons' is for '{nous}'! Use '{avez}' for vous: vous avez cherché.

concepts.definition: A small group of verbs makes the passé composé with {être}, not {avoir}. Most are about moving somewhere or changing state.

examples.fr: Hier, je suis allé au café.
examples.en: Yesterday I went to the café.

concepts.definition: Use the present of {être}, then the participle.
English speakers remember them with the name DR MRS VANDERTRAMP, one letter per verb. Many come in opposite pairs, like going in and going out.

examples.fr: Elles sont entrées dans le café.
Tu es monté dans le bus.

concepts.term: The ones you will use most
concepts.definition: Going, coming, leaving and arriving come up in every story.

examples.fr: Je suis resté à la maison.

concepts.definition: With {être}, the participle takes -e for a woman and -s for more than one person.
The form of {être} goes between {ne} and {pas}. It works the same way with {avoir}.

examples.fr: Je ne suis pas allé au café.
examples.en: I didn't go to the café.

mistakes.feedback: Venir uses ÊTRE! Use '{elle n'est pas venue}', not 'a pas venu'.
That's present tense! Use passé composé: elle n'est pas venue.

items/i-etes-entres.gloss: Did you go into the café?

mistakes.feedback: Entrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use '{êtes-vous entrés ?}' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: {êtes-vous entrés ?}
Rester uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use '{vous êtes restés}' (a DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: {vous êtes restés}.

vocabulary/elle-est-venue-ils-sont-venus.fr: elle est venue / ils sont venus
vocabulary/elle-est-venue-ils-sont-venus.note: with être the ending agrees: -e for feminine, -s for plural

vocabulary/il-est-ne-il-est-mort-fr.fr: il est né / il est mort
vocabulary/il-est-ne-il-est-mort-fr.note: naître → né, mourir → mort (both use être!)

concepts.definition: The participle of {avoir} is {eu}, said like the French letter u.

examples.fr: Nous avons eu de la chance.
Ils n'ont pas eu le temps.

concepts.definition: The participle of {être} is {été}, and it takes {avoir}.

examples.en: I went to the cinema yesterday.
examples.note: in everyday speech, {j'ai été} can mean I went

concepts.definition: The participle of {faire} is {fait}.
The participle of {voir} is {vu}.

examples.fr: Nous avons vu un bon film.
J'ai vu Paul, il est assis au café.
examples.en: I saw Paul, he's sitting at the café.

concepts.definition: These four participles come up in almost every story about the past.

examples.fr: Est-ce que vous avez vu le problème ?

concepts.definition: Like most verbs, these four make their past with {avoir}.
{vouloir} gives {voulu} and {pouvoir} gives {pu}. {devoir} gives {dû}, with an accent.

examples.fr: J'ai voulu partir, mais je n'ai pas pu.
examples.en: I wanted to leave, but I couldn't.

concepts.definition: The participle of {dire} is {dit}.
{prendre} gives {pris}, and the verbs built on it end the same way.
The participle of {mettre} is {mis}.

examples.fr: Nous avons mis nos livres sur la table.
examples.en: We put our books on the table.

concepts.definition: After these participles, the second verb stays in the infinitive.

examples.fr: J'ai voulu aller au cinéma, mais je n'ai pas eu le temps.
examples.en: I wanted to go to the cinema, but I didn't have time.

concepts.definition: Like most verbs, these make their past with {avoir}.
Set the scene, say what happened and give the reason.

examples.fr: Hier, il faisait beau, donc je suis allé au parc.
examples.en: Yesterday it was nice out, so I went to the park.

examples.fr: J'étais content parce que j'avais du temps.
examples.en: I was happy because I had time.

concepts.term: Building a story step by step
concepts.definition: Start with the scene, add an event, then give the reason for the next event.

examples.fr: Il faisait beau quand je suis sorti.
examples.en: It was nice out when I went out.

examples.fr: J'ai décidé d'aller au café parce que j'avais faim.
examples.en: I decided to go to the café because I was hungry.

concepts.definition: Use the imparfait with words for places to paint the picture.

examples.fr: Le café était près de l'école.
examples.en: The café was near the school.

examples.fr: Il y avait beaucoup de gens.
examples.en: There were a lot of people.

examples.fr: Ils étaient assis autour des tables.
examples.en: They were sitting around the tables.

concepts.definition: Words like {donc} and {comme} tie one event to the next.

examples.fr: Comme il faisait beau, je suis sorti.
examples.en: As it was nice out, I went out.

examples.fr: J'ai vu Marie, donc on a parlé.
examples.en: I saw Marie, so we talked.

examples.fr: On est allés au café car on avait faim.
examples.en: We went to the café because we were hungry.

concepts.definition: Put the events in order with {d'abord} and {ensuite}, and say where each one happened.

examples.fr: D'abord, je suis allé au café près de l'école.
examples.en: First I went to the café near the school.

examples.fr: Ensuite, j'ai vu Marie devant le cinéma.
examples.en: Then I saw Marie in front of the cinema.

examples.fr: Après, j'ai joué avec mon chien.
examples.en: After that I played with my dog.

concepts.term: A verb, then {de} or {à}, then a second verb
concepts.definition: Some verbs take a second verb after {de}, like {décider de}. Others take it after {à}, like {commencer à}.

examples.en: I decided to go to the café.
examples.note: the second verb stays in the infinitive

items/i-a-cause-de.text: ___ la fête, on est rentrés tard
items/i-a-cause-de.gloss: Because of the party, we got home late

mistakes.feedback: The party is the cause here, not a thanks. Use '{à cause de}'.
Use '{à cause de la fête}' (because of THE PARTY, a noun).

items/i-ai-fait-ensuite.text: J'___ mes devoirs ___ j'ai écouté de la musique
items/i-ai-fait-ensuite.gloss: I did my homework then I listened to music

mistakes.feedback: Completed homework = specific event! Use passé composé: j'ai fait.
'Car' is for reason! Use '{ensuite}' (then) for sequence.

items/i-grace-a.gloss: Thanks to you, I learned French

mistakes.feedback: Parce que needs a CLAUSE! Use '{Grâce à toi}' (thanks to you - NOUN).
Succeeding is POSITIVE! Use '{grâce à}' (not à cause de which is negative/neutral).

items/i-j-en-ai-mange.text: Il y avait du pain, alors j'en ___.
items/i-j-en-ai-mange.gloss: There was some bread, so I ate some.

mistakes.feedback: Eating the bread is the event, so use the passé composé: {j'en ai mangé}.

items/i-parce-que.gloss: Because I was hungry, I ate

mistakes.feedback: Grâce à is POSITIVE and needs a NOUN! Use '{Parce que}' + clause for hunger.
À cause de needs a NOUN! Use '{Parce que j'avais faim}' (because I was hungry).

items/i-sur-dans.text: Le livre était ___ la table ___ la cuisine
items/i-sur-dans.gloss: The book was on the table in the kitchen

mistakes.feedback: Wrong order! The book is ON (sur) the table, IN (dans) the room.
Au-dessus means 'above' (hanging). Use '{sur}' for '{on}' (touching surface).

concepts.definition: The passé composé tells what happened. The imparfait describes how things were or what used to happen.

examples.en: Yesterday I ate at the restaurant.

examples.fr: D'habitude, je mangeais à la maison.

concepts.definition: Use it for an event that started and finished: the main line of the story.

examples.fr: Hier matin, j'ai pris le bus.
examples.en: Yesterday morning I took the bus.

concepts.term: Imparfait: the scene and the habits
concepts.definition: Use it for descriptions, for states that went on and for things you used to do.

examples.fr: Je prenais le bus tous les matins.
examples.en: I used to take the bus every morning.

concepts.definition: Set the scene in the imparfait, then say what happened in the passé composé.

examples.fr: Il faisait beau quand je suis arrivé.
examples.en: It was nice out when I arrived.

examples.fr: Je prenais un café quand tu es arrivé.
examples.en: I was having a coffee when you arrived.

concepts.term: Words that point to each tense
concepts.definition: {hier} and {soudain} usually go with the passé composé. {tous les jours} and {d'habitude} go with the imparfait.

examples.fr: Hier, je suis allé au café.
examples.en: Yesterday I went to the café.

examples.fr: Je parlais français tous les jours.

examples.en: We usually went to the café.

concepts.definition: The imparfait says what was going on. The passé composé says what cut in.

examples.fr: Je parlais avec Marie quand tu as appelé.
examples.en: I was talking with Marie when you called.

examples.fr: Pendant que je mangeais, tu as appelé.
examples.en: While I was eating, you called.

concepts.definition: Age and a state that lasted take the imparfait. A feeling at one moment can take the passé composé.

items/i-jouais.text: Quand j'étais jeune, je ___ avec mon chien
items/i-jouais.gloss: When I was young, I used to play with my dog

mistakes.feedback: Repeated past action (habit)! Use imparfait: je jouais (I used to play).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: je jouais.

items/i-prenais-un-cafe.text: Je ___ un café quand tu es arrivé
items/i-prenais-un-cafe.gloss: I was having a coffee when you arrived

mistakes.feedback: Ongoing action (was having)! Use imparfait: je prenais.
That's present! Use imparfait for ongoing past: je prenais.

vocabulary/je-mangeais-fr.gloss: I was eating / I used to eat

2024-06-05-reading-9.description: A story in the past using passé composé, imparfait, causal words, and spatial prepositions - bringing together all of this unit

passage/b-bonjour-je-voulais-etre.fr: Il a dit: "Bonjour! Je voulais être dehors parce qu'il faisait si beau. Je suis content que tu sois là!"
passage/b-bonjour-je-voulais-etre.en: He said: "Hello! I wanted to be outside because it was so nice. I'm glad you're here!"

passage/b-marie-etait-notre-amie.fr: Marie était notre amie de la Sorbonne. Nous ne la voyons pas souvent parce qu'elle habite maintenant à Lyon. Grâce à cette rencontre, nous avons pu être ensemble pour l'après-midi.
passage/b-marie-etait-notre-amie.en: Marie was our friend from the Sorbonne. We don't see her often because she now lives in Lyon. Thanks to this meeting, we were able to be together for the afternoon.

passage/b-nous-avons-parle-pendant.fr: Nous avons parlé pendant une heure. Pierre voulait un nouveau travail à la Sorbonne parce qu'il n'aimait pas son travail. Je le comprenais, car j'ai eu le même problème l'année dernière.
passage/b-nous-avons-parle-pendant.en: We talked for an hour. Pierre wanted a new job at the Sorbonne because he didn't like his job. I understood him, because I had the same problem last year.

passage/b-parfois-les-meilleures-journee.fr: Parfois, les meilleures journées sont des surprises. Grâce à ma sortie au Jardin du Luxembourg, j'ai eu une très belle journée avec mes amis.
passage/b-parfois-les-meilleures-journee.en: Sometimes the best days are surprises. Thanks to my outing to Jardin du Luxembourg, I had a very beautiful day with my friends.

passage/b-quelle-surprise-elle-a.fr: Elle a dit: "Quelle surprise! Je ne savais pas que vous étiez ici!"
passage/b-quelle-surprise-elle-a.en: She said: "What a surprise! I didn't know you were here!"

passage/b-salut-pierre-qu-est.fr: J'ai demandé: "Salut Pierre! Qu'est-ce que tu fais ici?"
passage/b-salut-pierre-qu-est.en: I asked: "Hi Pierre! What are you doing here?"

2024-06-05-reading-9.title: Reading - {Une Histoire du Passé}

concepts.definition: With a plural subject, the reflexive pronoun can mean each other.
Each other needs at least two people, so the subject is plural, or {on} meaning we.
The form is the same for both meanings. The situation tells you which one is meant.

examples.note: or: we're getting each other ready

concepts.term: Seeing and talking to each other
concepts.definition: You hear these between friends all the time.
In the past, every reflexive verb uses {être}, never {avoir}.
As with other verbs that take {être}, the past participle agrees with the subject.
The reflexive pronoun comes before the form of {être}.
The same order words work in the past.

examples.fr: Ce matin, je me suis réveillé à sept heures.
examples.en: This morning I woke up at seven.

examples.fr: J'étais en retard, donc je me suis dépêché.
examples.en: I was late, so I hurried.

concepts.definition: Says what is in front of something or someone.

examples.en: I'm in front of the door.

examples.fr: La voiture est devant la maison.
examples.en: The car is in front of the house.

examples.fr: Il y a un arbre devant ma fenêtre.
examples.en: There's a tree in front of my window.

concepts.definition: Says what is behind something or someone.

examples.fr: Le chat est derrière le sofa.
examples.en: The cat is behind the sofa.

examples.fr: Il y a un jardin derrière la maison.
examples.en: There's a garden behind the house.

concepts.definition: Says what is between two things or two people.

examples.fr: Le café est entre l'école et le parc.
examples.en: The café is between the school and the park.

examples.fr: Entre toi et moi, c'est un secret.
examples.en: Between you and me, it's a secret.

concepts.definition: Says that someone or something is one of a group.

examples.fr: Ton livre est parmi mes livres.
examples.en: Your book is among my books.

examples.fr: Parmi les étudiants, il y a des Français.
examples.en: Among the students, there are some French people.

concepts.definition: Says what is higher than something. Before {le}, {de} becomes {du}.

examples.fr: Le tableau est au-dessus de la table.
examples.en: The painting is above the table.

concepts.definition: Says what is lower than something. On its own, {au-dessous} means downstairs.
Short words you already use to say where a thing is: inside something, on top of it or under it.

examples.fr: Le livre est dans le sac.
examples.en: The book is in the bag.

examples.fr: Mon téléphone est sur la table.
examples.en: My phone is on the table.

examples.fr: Le chien est sous la table.
examples.en: The dog is under the table.

mistakes.feedback: Au-dessus means 'above/upstairs'. Use '{au-dessous}' for 'below/downstairs'!
En bas works too! But we're learning '{au-dessous}' here.
Use '{au-dessus de}' for 'above'.
Devant means 'in front of'. Use '{au-dessus de}' for 'above'!

items/i-sous-2.gloss: The cat is under the car

mistakes.feedback: Sur means 'on top of'. Use '{sous}' for 'under/beneath'!
Dans means 'in/inside'. Use '{sous}' for 'under/beneath'!

items/i-sur.gloss: My phone is on the table

mistakes.feedback: Dans means 'in/inside'. Use '{sur}' for 'on top of' a surface!
Au-dessus means 'above' (not touching). Use '{sur}' for '{on}' (touching)!

parts/p-keep-the-article.heading: Keep the article
text: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, so learn each cognate with its article, {un} or {une}. French does not drop the article the way English does in “Coffee is good”.
parts/p-keep-the-article.note: Every time you recognize a cognate, you add a French word without studying it.

concepts.definition: The verb for giving things and information.
{donner} changes like {parler}.

concepts.term: Giving a number, giving you hunger
concepts.definition: You also give information with {donner}. {ça donne faim} means it makes you hungry.
{donner} and {prendre} are opposites.

examples.fr: Je donne le livre à Marie.
examples.en: I give the book to Marie.

concepts.definition: Use {à} before the person who gets the thing.

examples.fr: Je donne le livre à mon ami.
examples.en: I give the book to my friend.

concepts.definition: {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {ne} goes before the verb and {rien} after it.

mistakes.feedback: For nothing, {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {il ne dit rien}.
For nothing, {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {il ne donne rien}.

items/i-je-ne-fais-rien.situation: A friend asks {Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?} Say you're not doing anything.

mistakes.feedback: People often drop {ne} when they speak, but write it here: {je ne fais rien}.

accept: je ne fais rien du tout

mistakes.feedback: {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {je ne vois rien}.

concepts.definition: You are looking for something you have not found yet.
The verb for the moment the search ends and you have the thing.
{chercher} is the search and {trouver} is the result.
{chercher} already means to look for, so nothing goes between the verb and the thing.

sections/s-liaison-and-elision.heading: Words that run together
sections/s-liaison-and-elision.text: A silent final consonant is said before a vowel. A short word like {je} drops its vowel before another vowel.

examples.note: the s of {vous} is said as z

sections/s-nasal-vowels.heading: Nasal vowels
sections/s-nasal-vowels.text: French has vowels you say partly through the nose. English has none of them.

checks.ask: Which one means “I don't have a cat”?

options.text: Je ne ai pas de chat.

checks.why: After {pas}, {un} becomes {de}, and {ne} becomes {n'} before a vowel: {Je n'ai pas de chat.}

checks.ask: Which one means “You aren't a child”?

options.text: Tu ne pas es un enfant.

checks.why: {ne} goes before the verb and {pas} after it. After {être}, {un} stays as it is: {Tu n'es pas un enfant.}

checks.ask: Which one means “I don't have a car anymore”?
checks.why: {plus} takes the place of {pas} and means anymore.

concepts.definition: Each number up to 16 has its own word, so learn these by heart.
Say ten, then the number: 17 is ten-seven.
Learn the tens, then add the numbers 1 to 9 after them.
Put {et} between the ten and {un}, and a hyphen between the ten and 2 to 9. Before a feminine noun, {un} becomes {une}.

examples.fr: Elles ont cinquante et une voitures.

concepts.definition: French says 70 as sixty-ten and counts on with 11 to 19, so 75 is sixty-fifteen. Only 71 keeps {et}.
80 is four twenties, with an s that goes from 81 on, and there is no {et}. 90 to 99 add 10 to 19 to four twenties, and 100 is {cent}.
To give an age, French says you have that many years: {avoir}, the number, then {ans}.

examples.fr: Paul a trente et un ans.

examples.en: The house is a hundred years old.
